strengths: Methodology and originality: Layer-wise variance correction and variance-dependent learning rates provide concrete heuristics for exploring low-loss trajectories. Combining model-to-model traversal with movement toward smaller parameter norms is a potentially useful methodological contribution.

Empirical scope: The main experiments include 200 LeNet5, 40 ResNet18, and 10 CCT7 repetitions, with means and standard deviations reported. Additional architecture–dataset combinations in Appendix A.4 provide preliminary evidence of broader applicability.

Presentation and reproducibility: Algorithms 1–2, the geometric illustration, and Appendix A.6 provide substantial implementation detail, including layer schedules, optimization settings, preprocessing, hardware, and runtime.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript acknowledges failures for sharp starting minima, restrictions on layer variances, and deterioration of test performance along some paths. These disclosures are useful. The standard image-classification experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—global connectivity is unsupported: Successful connections between finitely many models trained with identical hyperparameters establish connectivity only among sampled endpoints, not the entire loss sublevel set. Section 3.2 explicitly restricts suitable starting points and reports failures for Adam-trained ResNet18 models. Model-to-origin trajectories likewise do not establish that arbitrary components connect across variance levels. The title and central conclusions therefore substantially exceed the evidence.

Soundness—continuous low-loss paths are not established even for the sampled pairs: The algorithms produce discrete checkpoints, without reporting dense interpolation checks or bounds between consecutive checkpoints. Retraining and subsequent variance correction can cross or introduce loss barriers. Figure 2 reports smoothed means and standard deviations rather than per-run maximum losses, while Appendix A.6 uses rolling training-loss stopping criteria. These measurements do not certify that the entire path stays within a fixed full-dataset loss sublevel set. Nonzero endpoint distances also leave the final connection to the destination unverified.

Soundness—the parameter-redundancy conclusion does not follow: Section 5 conflates the linear span of sampled parameter vectors with intrinsic dimension and functional nonredundancy. A lower-dimensional curved set can span the full ambient space. Moreover, for continuous loss, any point strictly below the threshold already has an open neighborhood inside the sublevel set, so full dimension does not rule out redundant parameters. No singular-value spectra, numerical rank tolerances, or sufficient sampling details accompany the SVD claim.

Mathematical presentation: Equation 2 does not define a sphere in the stated ambient space unless the parameter mean is fixed; adding a constant to every coordinate preserves variance, producing an unbounded set. Approximately zero means in sampled models do not repair the definition. The manuscript also repeatedly calls a loss sublevel set a 'subspace' and equates low-loss points with local minima, neither of which is generally valid.

Evaluation and originality: The claimed superiority to AutoNEB is based on published results under different conditions, including ResNet18 versus ResNet20 in Appendix A.7. There is no matched comparison using identical endpoints, architecture, loss evaluation, and computational budget. Ablations are also needed to distinguish the benefits of variance correction, layer scheduling, learning-rate scaling, and extensive additional training. Earlier mode-connectivity methods already construct paths in parameter space, weakening the claimed distinction of exploration in the 'full parameter space.'

Significance—generalization and efficiency claims remain inconclusive: The reported ImageNet improvement from 69.758% to 70.55% is promising, but lacks a compute-matched continued-training or weight-decay baseline, uncertainty estimates, and a clearly specified validation-based checkpoint-selection protocol. Appendix A.6 reports 340 GPU-hours for this experiment. Consequently, the results do not establish that the proposed exploration is a more efficient alternative to hyperparameter tuning or that connectivity explains the gain.

Interpretation: The PCA analysis attributes trajectory fluctuations to sharpness and input-feature frequencies without measuring curvature or feature sensitivity. Trajectory roughness can reflect stochastic optimization, step sizes, and projection. The associated claims about residual connections and layer-wise feature diagnostics are therefore speculative.

Reproducibility: Despite useful hyperparameter tables, the manuscript does not identify an accessible implementation of LLPF, although some settings are deferred to source code. Treatment of batch-normalization running statistics, the precise training-loss evaluation protocol, and the SVD experiment are insufficiently specified. These omissions directly affect the geometric and empirical claims.

strengths: The proposed variance-corrected model-to-model traversal and variance-dependent model-to-origin procedure offer concrete heuristics for exploring trained networks. Their practical usefulness is a plausible contribution, independently of the stronger geometric claims.

The empirical investigation includes convolutional and transformer architectures, with 200 LeNet5, 40 ResNet18, and 10 CCT7 repetitions reported for the main experiments. Figures 2–3 present training loss, parameter distances, and test behavior, providing useful observations beyond endpoint performance.

Presentation and reproducibility benefit from pseudocode and appendix tables covering layer schedules, optimization settings, preprocessing, architecture changes, and computational costs. The authors explicitly acknowledge failures from some starting models, normalization-layer exclusions, and deterioration in test performance along some paths. These disclosures are valuable; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—global connectivity is not established. Connecting finitely many models trained with identical hyperparameters supports connectivity among sampled endpoints, not the entire loss sublevel set asserted in the title and conclusions. Section 3.2 also restricts eligible starting points to flat regions and reports failures for Adam-trained ResNet18 models. Those failures do not establish disconnectedness, but they underscore the unsupported extrapolation. Model-to-origin trajectories likewise cannot rule out other disconnected components.

Soundness—even continuous connectivity of the sampled endpoints requires stronger validation. The algorithms return discrete checkpoints, without establishing that interpolating between consecutive checkpoints stays below a fixed loss threshold. Training followed by variance correction does not guarantee that the corrected point remains low-loss, and reaching a point near the destination does not certify the final connection. Figure 2 reports smoothed means and standard deviations, which cannot establish maximum loss across every trajectory. Full-dataset, unsmoothed checkpoint losses and dense segment evaluations are needed; rolling minibatch loss criteria are insufficient for Equation 1.

Soundness—the parameter-redundancy conclusion in Section 5 is invalid. The linear span of sampled parameter vectors is not the intrinsic dimension of their underlying set: a curved lower-dimensional set can span the ambient space. Moreover, for continuous loss, any point strictly below the threshold has an open neighborhood within the sublevel set, making full local dimension compatible with substantial functional parameter redundancy. The manuscript provides neither numerical singular-value spectra nor rank tolerances or sufficient sampling details to assess its SVD experiment.

Mathematical precision and presentation need substantial correction. Equation 2 defines a constant-variance set with unrestricted mean, which is an unbounded cylinder along the all-ones direction, not a sphere. A fixed-mean restriction would yield a sphere within a hyperplane. Approximate zero means in sampled models do not change the exact definition. The manuscript also calls a general sublevel set a 'subspace' and treats low-loss checkpoints as local minima without justification. These distinctions directly affect its geometric arguments.

Originality and comparative significance are insufficiently demonstrated. Mode connectivity and loss sublevel sets are established concepts already represented in the references; the potential novelty lies chiefly in the traversal heuristics. Appendix A.7 compares LLPF on ResNet18 with previously published AutoNEB results on ResNet20, without matching endpoints, architectures, optimization, or computational budgets. This cannot establish superior path quality. Controlled comparisons and ablations of variance correction, layer scheduling, and learning-rate scaling are missing.

The generalization and efficiency claims lack adequate controls. The reported ImageNet improvement from 69.758% to 70.55% is promising, but ordinary continued training and tuned weight-decay baselines are absent, so the benefit cannot be attributed to the proposed geometric exploration. Table 5 reports 340 GPU-hours for this experiment, making claims of improved efficiency especially premature. Repetition uncertainty and a validation-based checkpoint-selection protocol are also needed to assess the reported test-performance peak.

Several secondary claims remain speculative, and reproducibility is incomplete. Section 5 interprets oscillations in PCA trajectories as evidence of sharpness, input-frequency sensitivity, and residual-network feature propagation without direct measurements or controlled tests. Appendix A.6 refers readers to source code for omitted configurations, but the manuscript provides no identifiable repository for the proposed method. Batch-normalization state handling and the SVD procedure also need specification. Overall, the useful empirical heuristics do not compensate for unsupported central conclusions; substantial methodological revision is required before acceptance.

strengths: Originality: The combination of layerwise variance correction, staged movement toward another model, and variance-dependent learning rates provides a concrete heuristic for exploring trained-network parameter space. The model-to-origin procedure is a potentially useful extension of conventional endpoint-to-endpoint connectivity experiments.

Empirical scope: Figure 2 reports repeated experiments across substantially different architectures: 200 for LeNet5, 40 for ResNet18, and 10 for CCT7. These results provide useful evidence that the procedure can repeatedly find sequences of low-loss models under the tested training configurations.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides algorithm pseudocode, extensive hyperparameter and preprocessing tables, architecture modifications, and hardware/runtime information. It also candidly describes prerequisites, failures from some starting models, and deterioration in test performance along certain paths.

Significance: Post-training exploration toward smaller weight norms is worth investigating. The reported ImageNet accuracy improvement from 69.758% to 70.55% is encouraging, although the current controls do not establish its cause or comparative value.
weaknesses: Soundness—global connectivity is not established. The title, abstract, and Section 5 generalize from finitely many models trained with identical hyperparameters to the entire loss sublevel set. Such experiments can establish connectivity among sampled points, but cannot exclude other disconnected components. The acknowledged restrictions to flat starting regions and nearby layer variances further narrow the evidence. Model-to-origin trajectories do not establish that arbitrary components on different variance levels are connected.

Soundness—even the constructed continuous paths are insufficiently validated. Algorithms 1 and 2 return discrete iterates; low loss at those iterates does not establish low loss between them or on the final connection to the destination. Figure 2 reports smoothed means and standard deviations, which cannot certify a maximum-loss threshold for every run. The manuscript needs explicit interpolation checks, unsmoothed per-path maxima, endpoint residuals, and a clear distinction between full-dataset loss and stochastic training-loss estimates. Algorithm 1 also applies variance correction after retraining without an explicit loss check.

Soundness—the parameter-redundancy conclusion is invalid. Section 5 conflates the rank of sampled parameter vectors, the intrinsic dimension of a set, and functional parameter redundancy. A curved lower-dimensional set can have a full-dimensional linear span. Moreover, for continuous loss, any point strictly below the threshold already has a full-dimensional neighborhood within the sublevel set, regardless of redundant parameters. Thus the reported SVD observation does not demonstrate that all parameters are necessary. Sample counts, singular-value spectra, centering, and numerical rank tolerances are also missing.

Mathematical presentation: Equation 2 defines a constant-variance set, which is unbounded along the all-ones direction and is not a sphere in the full layer parameter space unless the mean is fixed. The exact relation is ||w||² = n Var(w) + n mean(w)²; small absolute means alone do not quantify the approximation error. Calling general loss sublevel sets 'subspaces' and identifying low-loss points with local minima in Section 5 introduce further substantive conceptual errors.

Comparative evaluation and originality: Appendix A.7 compares LLPF on ResNet18 with a published AutoNEB result on ResNet20, rather than matching architecture, endpoints, loss evaluation, and computation. This does not establish superior path quality. There are no controlled ablations isolating variance correction, layer ordering, or learning-rate scaling, and no direct comparison with the cited alternative path-construction methods. Defining a deterministic loss sublevel set is itself standard, so the methodological advance needs stronger isolation.

Significance and generalization: The ImageNet gain is not compared with equal-budget continued training, tuned weight decay, or fine-tuning with normalization parameters excluded from decay. Table 5 reports 340 GPU-hours for this experiment, making the claimed efficiency advantage particularly unsubstantiated. The manuscript also does not specify an independent validation-based checkpoint-selection protocol or uncertainty across repetitions for Figure 5.

Interpretation: The PCA trajectory plots do not establish landscape sharpness, input-frequency sensitivity, or the proposed effect of residual connections. Those conclusions require curvature measurements, frequency-controlled experiments, and architectural controls; optimizer dynamics and projection effects are alternative explanations.

Reproducibility and limitations: Despite useful implementation tables, the SVD experiment is not reproducibly specified, batch-normalization state handling along paths is unclear, and some configurations are deferred to source code without an identifiable submission-code link. The disclosed algorithmic limitations are helpful, but the central conclusions do not respect them. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by unsupported central claims and inadequate comparative validation.

strengths: Significance: Constructing connections between independently initialized models is a useful problem. The experiments extend empirical coverage to structurally diverse architectures, including MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, DLA, RegNet, and CCT, rather than relying exclusively on conventional ResNets.

Originality: Combining layer-wise movement, variance correction, and a variance-dependent learning rate provides a plausible algorithmic contribution. The two-stage construction for models trained with different weight decay values is an interesting extension.

Soundness: The paper includes repeated experiments, parameter-distance trajectories, and explicit interpolation checks. Figure 5 evaluates 50 interpolation samples per segment, with additional checks in Appendix A.7; these are valuable evidence beyond merely showing low-loss discrete checkpoints.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides pseudocode, detailed configurations for several architectures, preprocessing choices, model modifications, and reference runtimes. The organization generally makes the intended procedure understandable.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly reports deterioration in test performance along some paths and distinguishes training-loss connectivity from generalization. This appropriately limits practical interpretations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—comparative claims are unsupported: No existing method is evaluated on the same endpoint pairs, architectures, and computational budgets. Table 1 juxtaposes results from different papers and different ResNet variants, explicitly acknowledging that their losses are not comparable. Consequently, the claims that LLPF improves architectural applicability and reliability over prior methods remain unestablished. Not having previously tested an architecture does not demonstrate that a baseline cannot connect it.

Soundness—path validation is incomplete: Figure 2 reports training loss averaged over training rounds near M3, whereas the returned checkpoint is Pi+1 after another variance correction. These measurements do not directly establish the full-training-set loss of every returned checkpoint. Smoothing means and standard deviations also cannot establish worst-case barriers or success rates. The interpolation experiments partially address this issue, but cover selected configurations, and Figure 5 changes the hyperparameters from Figure 2. A consistent evaluation should report unsmoothed maximum full-data loss for checkpoints and interpolated segments across all evaluated runs.

Soundness—endpoint connectivity needs stronger verification: Algorithm 1 preserves the starting layer variances, while destination variances are only approximately equal. Exact convergence to the destination is therefore generally incompatible with the constraint. Section 5 accepts residual layer-wise distances below 0.1, without validating the final segment to the actual destination. For the different-weight-decay experiments, loss and accuracy curves alone likewise do not demonstrate arrival at the specified endpoint. Endpoint residuals and final-segment loss checks are needed.

Originality and mechanism: There are no controlled ablations isolating variance correction, layer ordering, the FDF strategy, or AngleConformal learning-rate scaling. Since layer-wise connectivity is already established in cited work, the experiments do not identify which proposed components provide the advance. The claim that only layer selection and ordering determine success also lacks a systematic sensitivity study.

Mathematical presentation: Equation 2 does not define a sphere in the full parameter space: variance is invariant under adding a constant to every coordinate, so the constant-variance set is unbounded along the all-ones direction. A sphere interpretation requires fixing the mean. Equation 3 also incorrectly presents equal empirical variance across independent random initializations as an exact identity. These issues do not automatically invalidate the heuristic, but they weaken its geometric justification and should be corrected.

Reproducibility and reliability: The pseudocode omits the central layer-selection schedule, and the text describes one-layer-at-a-time operation while Table 2 uses progressively expanding layer subsets. It is unclear which parameters are moved, trained, or frozen at each stage. Batch-normalization running-statistic handling during interpolation and evaluation is also unspecified. The reported repetitions are encouraging, but exact run counts, failure criteria, unsuccessful attempts, and tuning procedures are needed to substantiate consistency. The manuscript refers to supplementary code, which could not be assessed from the supplied PDF.

Significance and practical scope: Table 6 reports approximately 21–24 H100 hours for individual ResNet18/CCT connections and 45 RTX 5090 hours for DLA. Without matched-budget comparisons, the benefit of this substantial computation is unclear. Evaluation remains limited to MNIST and CIFAR-scale tasks, and heterogeneous-training evidence concerns weight-decay changes rather than broadly different training configurations. These limitations narrow the contribution; the decisive reason for rejection is the unresolved comparative and path-validity evidence.

strengths: Originality: Combining layer-wise path construction, variance correction, and variance-dependent learning rates is a plausible methodological contribution. The model-to-origin component also offers an interesting way to connect solutions with different parameter scales.

Significance: The architectural coverage is useful, including MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, and CCT, with experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. This extends empirical investigation beyond the small set of architectures commonly studied.

Soundness: The authors report at least ten repetitions of the principal experiments and provide interpolation checks with 50 samples per segment for selected configurations (Figure 5 and Appendix A.7). These checks provide meaningful evidence beyond merely observing low-loss discrete iterates.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides pseudocode, training configurations, preprocessing details, layer schedules, and computational costs. It explicitly acknowledges deterioration in test performance along some paths; this honest limitation does not invalidate a contribution about training-loss connectivity. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—comparative claims are unsupported. No controlled experiments compare LLPF with existing path-finding methods on the same endpoints, architectures, loss criteria, and computational budgets. Table 1 compares losses from different ResNet variants and acknowledges their incompatibility. Prior methods not having reported experiments on particular architectures or hyperparameters does not establish that LLPF overcomes a limitation of those methods. This is a central gap because broader applicability and greater consistency are the principal advertised advances.

Soundness—the principal measurements do not fully establish the claimed paths. Figure 2 reports training loss averaged over the final optimization rounds near M3, whereas the returned point Pi+1 follows an additional variance-correction operation. Thus, this measurement does not directly verify the full-dataset loss at the returned points. Smoothed averages also do not establish worst-case path loss. The interpolation experiments partially address this concern, but cover selected configurations, with Figure 5 explicitly using changed hyperparameters. The paper should evaluate unsmoothed full-training-set losses at returned points and interpolated segments, including the final segment to the exact destination; small per-layer endpoint distances alone do not certify that segment.

Soundness and originality—the explanation of what makes LLPF work lacks controlled ablations. The manuscript attributes success primarily to layer-wise connectivity and emphasizes variance correction, FDF ordering, and adaptive learning rates, but does not systematically isolate their contributions. In particular, it remains unclear how much improvement comes from these choices versus the extensive local retraining budget.

Soundness—the variance geometry is incorrectly defined. Equation 2 does not define a sphere in the full parameter space: adding any constant to every coordinate preserves variance, making the set unbounded in the all-ones direction. A sphere arises only after fixing the mean in the corresponding subspace. The approximately zero-mean observation can motivate a heuristic, but does not repair the exact definition, especially because VarianceCorrection preserves the current mean. Equation 3 also treats sampled initialization variances as exactly equal rather than distinguishing empirical variance from the variance of the generating distribution.

Reliability claims exceed the reported evidence. Repeated experiments and shaded deviations are helpful, but the paper does not provide explicit success counts, a prespecified success criterion, or a clear account of endpoint selection and tuning across pairs. The requirement for flat starting regions is not operationalized, and near-zero training loss does not by itself establish flatness. Consequently, statements about seed-independent consistency remain conditional and insufficiently quantified.

Significance and reproducibility are limited by cost and specification gaps. Table 6 reports approximately 21–24 H100 hours for individual ResNet18/CCT connections, without matched baseline timing. The practical advantage is therefore unclear. Although appendix configurations are substantial, the pseudocode does not explicitly integrate layer scheduling or explain normalization-buffer handling and evaluation along interpolations. Code is said to be supplementary, but was not included in the supplied material and could not be assessed.

Scope and presentation need tighter qualification. Different-training-hyperparameter experiments vary weight decay, which supports a narrower conclusion than general hyperparameter robustness. Likewise, architectural diversity on small image datasets does not establish scalability to modern large models. The text describes processing one layer at a time, while Table 2 uses cumulative groups of layers; this discrepancy obscures an essential implementation choice.

strengths: Significance: Constructing paths between independently initialized models is a worthwhile problem. The experiments cover a useful range of architectures, including MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, and CCT, with additional CIFAR-100 results beyond the main CIFAR-10 evaluation.

Originality: Combining layer-wise movement, variance correction, local retraining, and a variance-reduction stage provides a potentially useful empirical recipe. Connecting models trained with different weight decay values is an interesting extension, demonstrated for DLA, ResNet18, and CCT.

Soundness: The paper makes meaningful verification efforts: repeated experiments with at least ten mode pairs, layer-wise endpoint-distance measurements, and interpolation checks with 50 samples per segment for selected settings. These support the feasibility of the approach in those settings.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall construction is understandable, and Appendix A.5 provides substantial training, preprocessing, scheduling, and hardware/runtime information. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges deterioration in test performance; this honest limitation is valuable. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central comparative claims lack controlled evidence. Table 1 compares published results from different architectures and training setups rather than running AutoNEB, optimized polygonal/Bézier paths, or SPRO on the same endpoint pairs. Its caveat about incomparable losses is appropriate, but the table cannot establish superior applicability, consistency, or path quality. In particular, failure to report consistency in prior work is not evidence that those methods are inconsistent.

Soundness—the principal measurements do not fully establish continuous low-loss connections. Figure 2 reports training losses averaged over the final retraining rounds near M3, whereas the returned point Pi follows another variance correction that can change loss. Curves and uncertainty bands are also smoothed. The interpolation checks are valuable but cover only selected configurations, with changed hyperparameters for CCT. Report unsmoothed, full-training-set maximum losses at returned points and interpolation samples, and explicitly validate the final segment from the approximate endpoint to the actual destination.

Soundness—the geometric definition is incorrect as written. Equation 2 defines a constant-variance set without fixing the mean; it is unbounded along the all-ones direction, rather than a sphere. Exactly, ||w||² = n Var(w) + n Mean(w)². A near-zero-mean approximation can motivate a spherical picture for some weights, but does not make Equation 2 a sphere, and VarianceCorrection preserves a potentially changing mean. Equation 3 likewise treats equal initialization-distribution variances as exact equality of realized sample variances. These statements need correction and their relevance to normalization parameters and biases needs clarification.

Originality and attribution: There are no controlled ablations separating the effects of layer scheduling, variance correction, retraining budget, and learning-rate rescaling. Consequently, the paper does not establish which ingredients explain its success or how much they improve on simpler layer-wise movement with retraining. The related-work discussion also conflates FGE with the separately optimized connecting curves in Garipov et al., weakening the baseline framing.

Reliability and reproducibility: Similar mean trajectories with standard-deviation bands do not establish the claimed seed-independent reliability. The paper needs exact trial counts, explicit success criteria, per-run maximum barriers, failures, and the hyperparameter-selection protocol. The manuscript also leaves unclear whether layer selection restricts movement, retraining, or both, and how batch-normalization running statistics are handled during path construction and evaluation. Code is said to be supplementary, but was not available in the supplied material.

Significance and scope: Broad architectural coverage is promising, but all evaluations remain on MNIST/CIFAR-scale tasks. The different-hyperparameter claim is supported specifically by weight-decay changes, not broader optimizer or training variations. Computational cost is substantial: Table 6 reports approximately 21–24 H100 hours for representative connections. Without matched-budget baselines, the practical value relative to existing methods remains uncertain.

Presentation: Figure 1's caption overlaps the following paragraph on page 6, several plots and tables are difficult to read, and some appendix captions misidentify the plotted architectures. More substantively, the description of operating one layer at a time does not clearly explain the cumulative multi-layer schedules in Table 2. These issues make an already configuration-sensitive algorithm harder to reproduce.

strengths: Significance: Constructing reliable low-loss connections between independently initialized networks is a useful research objective. The evaluation covers a substantial variety of architectures, including MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, and CCT, with additional CIFAR100 and ImageNet10 experiments.

Originality: Combining progressive layer selection, variance correction, local retraining, and a variance-dependent learning rate provides a plausible algorithmic contribution. Connecting models trained with different hyperparameters is a useful extension, illustrated for three architectures.

Soundness: The paper includes repeated experiments for the main settings, component ablations in Appendix I, and interpolation checks with 50 samples per segment in Figure 5. These provide meaningful evidence that the method can construct low-loss trajectories in selected settings.

Presentation and transparency: The algorithms, geometric illustration, and extensive configuration tables help explain the approach. The authors acknowledge increased test loss, computational expense, and difficulties with outward variance exploration. The path-connectedness discussion is explicitly framed as a conjecture. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline conclusions are not adequately supported. Appendix C establishes that rerunning a script without changing its default seed produces correlated models; this does not establish that the original Garipov et al. experiments used that procedure or that their method is restricted to nearby modes. One independently seeded VGG pair with high path loss cannot justify the categorical dismissal. Table 9 compares AutoNEB on ResNet20 against LLPF on ResNet18, using approximately 6.5 versus 21 H100 hours, while Table 1 additionally mixes architectures and published results. Appendix J supplies a useful same-pair example, but selects it from a larger pool without reporting aggregate comparative success. Matched endpoints, architectures, tuning effort, and computational budgets are needed to establish superiority.

Soundness—the principal measurements do not establish the claimed worst-case loss along the returned paths. Figure 2 reports training loss averaged over final retraining steps near M3, whereas the returned point Pi follows another variance correction. Curves and uncertainty bands are further smoothed. These quantities need not bound the full-dataset loss at returned vertices or between them. The interpolation experiments are valuable, but cover selected settings, and Figure 5 explicitly changes the hyperparameters. Report unsmoothed per-run maximum losses on the actual returned paths under a consistent evaluation protocol.

Soundness—connection to the actual destination remains insufficiently verified. Algorithm 1 preserves starting-layer variances although destination variances differ, so exact endpoint convergence generally cannot follow from this constraint. Section 5 accepts residual layer distances below 0.1 without validating the final segment to D. Figure 9 explicitly reports up to threefold variance differences for RegNet, making this more than a negligible approximation. Similar endpoint test performance is not evidence of parameter-space connection. An explicit low-loss final bridge is necessary.

Reliability and reproducibility: The broad consistency claim exceeds the reported evidence. Figure 10 states that most additional settings were run only once; the paper does not provide a comprehensive success-rate table with predefined thresholds, all attempted pairs, and tuning budgets. Although configuration tables are helpful, the abstract's source-code availability statement has no URL. The supplied manuscript also leaves important implementation details unclear, including normalization-buffer handling during interpolation, which parameters retraining updates in each phase, and the ImageNet10 construction and preprocessing.

Mathematical presentation: Equation 2 defines a constant-variance set, which is unbounded along the all-ones direction rather than a sphere unless the mean is fixed. Approximate zero means can motivate a norm approximation, but do not make the stated set a sphere. Equation 3 also confuses equal initialization-distribution variance with exactly equal empirical variance of independently sampled weights. These distinctions matter because the geometric interpretation underlies both algorithms and their endpoint arguments.

Significance and originality remain incompletely established relative to the cost. Table 8 reports approximately 21–24 H100 hours for representative connections and thousands of equivalent training epochs. Such costs can be acceptable for landscape analysis, but require a demonstrated advantage over adequately tuned alternatives. The ablations support individual components but do not isolate the proposed layer-ordering strategy against alternative orders or sufficiently distinguish the contribution from the cited layer-wise connectivity work. The promising empirical idea therefore needs stronger comparative and path-validity evidence before others can reliably build on its central claims.

strengths: Significance: Constructing low-loss paths between independently initialized networks is a useful research problem. The evaluation spans substantially different architectures, including DLA, mobile CNNs, and CCT, with additional CIFAR100 and ImageNet10 experiments.

Originality: Combining layer-wise movement, variance correction, and local retraining provides a potentially useful empirical procedure. The model-to-origin component also enables examples connecting models trained with different hyperparameters.

Soundness: The manuscript includes substantial supporting experiments: at least ten repetitions for the principal settings, component ablations in Appendix I, and interpolation checks with 50 samples per segment in Figure 5 and Appendix H. Appendix J provides a concrete endpoint pair for which LLPF improves upon AutoNEB.

Presentation and transparency: The geometric illustration, pseudocode, training recipes, and runtime tables help explain the method. The authors acknowledge worsening test performance, computational costs, and limitations of movement toward the origin, and appropriately describe universal connectivity as a conjecture. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline conclusions exceed the evidence. Appendix C establishes that repeating a command with its default seed produces correlated endpoints; this does not establish that the original published experiments used those endpoints or that the method inherently cannot connect independent models. One unsuccessful independently seeded VGG experiment cannot justify that categorical conclusion. Tables 1 and 9 compare different architectures and unequal computational budgets: LLPF uses ResNet18 and 21 H100 hours, while AutoNEB uses ResNet20 and roughly 6.5 hours. Appendix J offers a useful selected counterexample, but not an aggregate, matched-budget comparison. These results do not establish the claimed general superiority in reliability or maximum path loss.

Soundness—the principal loss measurements do not directly certify the claimed paths. Figure 2 reports training loss averaged near M3, before the final variance correction that produces the actual returned point Pi+1. Curves and standard-deviation boundaries are additionally smoothed, which can conceal peaks. The interpolation checks are valuable but cover selected settings, with changed hyperparameters for Figure 5. The main experiments need unsmoothed full-training-set losses at returned points and interpolated segments, per-run maxima, and success rates against a specified threshold.

Soundness—connection to the destination remains approximate. Algorithm 1 preserves the starting layer variances, whereas independent endpoints have only approximately equal variances. Section 5 accepts residual layer distances below 0.1 and similar endpoint test losses as evidence of a valid connection; neither establishes a low-loss connection to the exact destination. The final segment from the returned point to D should be explicitly evaluated.

Technical formulation: Equation 2's fixed-variance set is not a sphere in the stated ambient space: adding a constant to every coordinate preserves variance, producing an unbounded direction. Restricting the mean would yield a sphere in a subspace, but the variance-correction operation preserves the current mean rather than enforcing such a restriction. The near-zero-mean approximation motivates a useful heuristic but does not make the formal definition correct. Treatment of normalization parameters also requires clarification because they are excluded from the supporting variance analysis but included in Algorithm 1's layer schedules.

Reproducibility and presentation: The abstract's source-code availability statement has no link in the supplied manuscript. Although many hyperparameters are documented, Algorithm 1 omits the central layer-selection procedure, and the relationship between its layer-wise description and the cumulative phase schedules is insufficiently explicit. Handling of batch-normalization running statistics during movement, retraining, and interpolation is not specified. These details materially affect reproduction of the reported paths.

Significance and originality remain incompletely established. Layer-wise connectivity is an acknowledged prior idea, but the paper lacks a direct comparison establishing the advance over that approach or a broadly replicated ablation isolating the variance mechanism. Practical utility is constrained by 21–45-hour connection runs in Table 8, and reliability beyond the principal CIFAR10 settings is less established: Figure 10 reports only three repetitions for two settings and single runs elsewhere. The contribution has clear empirical merits, but the unresolved validation and comparison issues prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Significance: A reliable method for connecting independently initialized networks would be a useful tool for studying loss geometry. LLPF provides promising demonstrations across CNN families and CCT, with additional CIFAR-100 and ImageNet10 experiments.

Originality: Combining layer-wise movement, variance correction, and local retraining is a useful methodological synthesis. The model-to-origin procedure also enables interesting demonstrations connecting models trained with different learning rates and weight decay.

Soundness: The paper includes meaningful supporting experiments: at least ten repetitions for the main settings, component ablations in Appendix I, and interpolation checks with 50 samples per segment in Figure 5. Appendix J supplies a concrete CCT pair where LLPF substantially improves on AutoNEB.

Presentation and transparency: The overall procedure is understandable, and Appendix F provides substantial training and search configurations and runtime information. The authors appropriately acknowledge increased test loss, computational costs, and the conjectural status of universal connectivity. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline comparisons do not establish the central superiority claim. Table 1 compares different architectures and training recipes; Table 9 compares 21-hour LLPF on ResNet18 against roughly 6.5-hour AutoNEB on ResNet20. Appendix J offers a selected matched-pair example, but no aggregate, compute-controlled comparison. Appendix C establishes that repeating a default command preserves initialization; this does not establish that the original publication used identical seeds or that its curve-fitting method generally cannot connect independent modes. SPRO is discussed but not evaluated.

Soundness—reported training losses do not consistently measure the claimed path. Figure 2 averages losses from the final retraining rounds near M3, whereas the returned point Pi is obtained after another variance correction. Curves and uncertainty boundaries are also smoothed. These measurements cannot establish worst-case full-training-set loss at the returned points. The interpolation experiments are valuable but cover selected settings, with modified hyperparameters for Figure 5. Unsmooth full-dataset evaluations of the actual paths are needed to substantiate the headline maximum-loss and reliability claims.

Soundness—reaching the exact destination remains unresolved. Section 5 accepts residual layer distances below 0.1, but proximity alone does not validate the final segment to D. Projection onto the starting variance constraint prevents exact convergence when endpoint variances differ. Figure 9 explicitly reports up to threefold variance differences for RegNet. The paper should evaluate the terminal connecting segment and specify how such mismatches are handled before claiming a complete connection.

Mathematical precision: Equation 2 defines a fixed-variance cylinder along the all-ones direction, not a sphere unless the mean is fixed. VarianceCorrection preserves the current mean rather than imposing a common one. Equation 3 likewise confuses identical initialization distributions with identical realized sample variances. These issues need correction and a clearer separation between heuristic geometry and established properties.

Reproducibility and presentation: The abstract's source-code availability statement contains no URL. Algorithm 1 omits the layer schedule from its pseudocode, and it is unclear which parameters are retrained versus moved or projected, how normalization buffers are handled, and whether the movement vector is normalized. ImageNet10 selection and preprocessing are not specified. These details materially affect independent reconstruction and loss evaluation.

Significance and evidential scope: Reliability is broader in the claims than in the evidence. Most additional CIFAR-100/ImageNet10 configurations in Figure 10 have only one run, and no comprehensive success-rate table or systematic hyperparameter-sensitivity study is provided. The substantial computation reported in Table 8 further limits practical utility without a demonstrated quality-versus-compute advantage. The promising empirical contribution therefore needs stronger validation before acceptance.
